$comment: Circular Words: the answers in play order (word N = task N). Each word has an English explanation that is shown after the game. Add new words at the end; reordering changes the task numbers.

words.meaning: To use something again instead of throwing it away after one use.
words.circular: Reuse is one of the “inner loops” of the circular economy: a refillable bottle or a school-uniform swap keeps a product in use without making anything new.

words.meaning: Our planet, the world we live on.
words.circular: The handbooks talk about “Spaceship Earth” and Earth Overshoot Day – the day each year when we have used more resources than the Earth can renew in a whole year.

words.meaning: A hard, clear material made by melting sand.
words.circular: Glass can be melted and recycled again and again without losing quality, so glass bottles and jars go into their own sorting bin.

words.meaning: A common food made from flour, water and yeast and baked in an oven.
words.circular: Bread is one of the most wasted foods. Some breweries now use surplus bread from bakeries to brew beer – an example of food upcycling.

words.meaning: Costing little money; often also low in quality.
words.circular: The linear economy runs on cheap materials, cheap energy and cheap labour. Fast fashion makes clothes so cheap that people treat them as disposable.

words.meaning: Having the colour of grass; also: good for the environment.
words.circular: The European Green Deal is the EU’s plan to make Europe climate-neutral by 2050. Watch out for “greenwashing” – false green claims on products.

words.meaning: Things we throw away because we no longer want or need them.
words.circular: The linear economy follows “take – make – waste”. A circular economy designs waste out from the start and treats what is left as a resource.

words.meaning: The clear liquid in rivers, lakes and seas that all life needs.
words.circular: Making products uses huge amounts of water, for example to grow cotton for clothes. Wasting food or clothes also wastes the water used to make them.

words.meaning: A hard, shiny material such as iron, copper, gold or aluminium.
words.circular: Metals can be recycled many times. Old phones and laptops contain gold, silver and copper, which is why e-waste is called an “urban mine”.

words.meaning: Recently made, picked or bought; not old, frozen or spoiled.
words.circular: Fresh food goes off quickly, so people often buy too much and throw it away. Households cause more than half of all food waste in the EU.

words.meaning: The amount of money you have to pay for something.
words.circular: A deposit adds a small price to bottles and cans that you get back when you return them. Germany’s “Pfand” system collects over 98% of bottles this way.

words.meaning: Something that the law says you are allowed to have or do.
words.circular: The EU “Right to Repair” makes producers keep products like phones and tablets easy to fix, with spare parts available for years.

words.meaning: A series of events that repeat in the same order.
words.circular: The butterfly diagram has two cycles: the biological cycle (food, wood and cotton return to nature) and the technical cycle (metals and plastics are kept in use).

words.meaning: One of the very large areas of salt water that cover most of the Earth.
words.circular: Millions of tonnes of plastic end up in the ocean, where it harms sea animals and breaks into microplastics that enter the food chain.

words.meaning: Thin material made from wood, used for writing, printing and packaging.
words.circular: Paper is made from wood fibres and can be recycled several times. Funny fact: the plastic bag was invented to replace paper bags and save trees!

words.meaning: The sweet part of a plant that holds its seeds, such as an apple or an orange.
words.circular: A lot of fruit is wasted only because it looks “ugly”. Leftover fruit pulp from juice factories can be upcycled into healthy snacks.

words.meaning: The name of a product or company that people recognise.
words.circular: Some fashion brands now offer repair services, take-back schemes or resale platforms, so that clothes stay in use for longer.

words.meaning: A number or score that shows the level of something.
words.circular: France’s repairability index gives products like phones a score out of 10, so buyers can see how easy they are to fix.

words.meaning: To use something together with other people.
words.circular: Sharing is one of the tightest loops of the circular economy: car-sharing, tool libraries and shared wardrobes mean fewer new products have to be made.

words.meaning: Poisonous; harmful to people, animals or nature.
words.circular: E-waste contains toxic substances like lead and mercury. Burning it in the open releases toxic fumes that are dangerous, especially for children.

words.meaning: A strong metal made from iron, used for buildings, cars and tools.
words.circular: Steel and cement cause a big share of global emissions. Recovering steel from old buildings and recycling it saves energy and raw materials.

words.meaning: A round fruit with red, green or yellow skin.
words.circular: In the biological cycle, apple cores from school lunch go into a compost bin, and the compost later feeds the soil in the school garden.

words.meaning: A new style or fashion that many people follow for a while.
words.circular: Fast fashion follows trends so quickly that clothes are thrown away after a short time. The EU campaign “ReSet the Trend” asks young people to change this.

words.meaning: A number that shows how good or bad something is.
words.circular: A repair score tells you how easy a product is to fix. Would you still buy a phone with a repair score of 3 out of 10?

words.meaning: How much something is worth, in money or in usefulness.
words.circular: A circular economy keeps products and materials at their highest value for as long as possible, instead of letting them lose all value as waste.

words.meaning: Coming from the sun or using the energy of the sun.
words.circular: Solar panels make renewable electricity. A circular economy should run on renewable energy like solar and wind instead of fossil fuels.

words.meaning: A device you use to call, send messages and use apps.
words.circular: A smartphone contains over 60 chemical elements. Modular phones can be repaired by swapping one part, and old phones should be recycled, not left in a drawer.

words.meaning: A small piece of paper or text on a product that gives information about it.
words.circular: Labels help us sort waste into the right bin and understand food dates: “use by” is about safety, “best before” is only about quality.

words.meaning: A shop; as a verb, to keep something for later.
words.circular: IKEA buys back used furniture for store credit and sells it again. Storing food properly at home also helps to stop food waste.

words.meaning: A row of connected things, like the metal rings of a chain.
words.circular: A supply chain or value chain is every step from raw material to finished product. Circular thinking looks at the whole chain, not just at the shop.

words.meaning: Connected with towns and cities.
words.circular: Old electronics are called “urban mines” because they are full of valuable metals that can be recovered instead of digging new mines.

words.meaning: Trousers made of denim.
words.circular: The company MUD Jeans lets customers lease jeans for a monthly fee. When the jeans wear out, they go back to be recycled.

words.meaning: A flat board on a wall or in a shop where you put things.
words.circular: “Shelf life” is how long food stays good. Packaging can extend it: a wrapped cucumber stays fresh for up to 14 days instead of 3.

words.meaning: Something you do regularly, often without thinking.
words.circular: Small daily habits – a reusable bottle, sorting waste, buying less – add up. In Germany, returning bottles for a deposit has become a cultural habit.

words.meaning: A simple picture or plan that explains how something works.
words.circular: The butterfly model shows the circular economy. The old linear model is “take – make – dispose”; new business models include renting and repair.

words.meaning: A large amount of water covering land that is usually dry.
words.circular: In the 1990s, plastic bags blocked drains in Bangladesh and made floods much worse. In 2002 it became the first country to ban thin plastic bags.

words.meaning: Strong cotton cloth, usually blue, used to make jeans.
words.circular: Durable materials like denim suit a circular wardrobe because they last a long time and can be repaired, rented or resold.

words.meaning: To notice something with your nose.
words.circular: Before you throw away food after its “best before” date, try the Look, Smell, Taste test – it is often still perfectly safe to eat.

words.meaning: From or in the area near you.
words.circular: Local repair shops, Repair Cafés and local food reduce transport and create jobs in your own community.

words.meaning: To shut something; to bring something to an end.
words.circular: To “close the loop” means bringing materials back into use, for example turning returned plastic bottles into new food-grade bottles.

words.meaning: A hard material formed by tiny sea animals; it builds reefs.
words.circular: Plastic debris covers and damages coral reefs, which are home to a huge variety of sea life.

words.meaning: A piece of clothing for the top part of the body.
words.circular: The “learning journey of a T-shirt” follows it from a cotton field to a factory, to your wardrobe and finally to a landfill – or, better, to reuse.

words.meaning: To try food or drink in your mouth to find out its flavour.
words.circular: The last step of the Look, Smell, Taste test: if “best before” food looks and smells fine, taste a little. Never do this with “use by” food!

words.meaning: Shapes like circles; ways that lead back to the beginning.
words.circular: In the butterfly diagram, the inner loops (sharing, repair, reuse) are better than the outer loop (recycling) because they keep the whole product.

words.meaning: Very simple plants that grow in water, like seaweed.
words.circular: Designers are making new biodegradable materials based on algae and fungi, which can safely return to nature at the end of their life.

words.meaning: A thin tube for drinking.
words.circular: Plastic straws, cutlery and plates are banned in the EU by the Single-Use Plastics Directive, because paper or reusable alternatives exist.

words.meaning: Things you throw away; rubbish.
words.circular: The aim of the circular economy is to keep materials out of the trash. “Wish-cycling” – putting the wrong things in the recycling bin – makes recycling harder.

words.meaning: Living things such as mushrooms and moulds.
words.circular: Fungi break down dead plants and return nutrients to the soil. Some new biodegradable materials are even based on fungi.

words.meaning: A wire covered in plastic that carries electricity or data.
words.circular: Before the EU common charger law, homes had drawers full of different cables. Now new phones, tablets and cameras all use USB-C, which cuts e-waste.

words.meaning: To make something new again, or to replace it.
words.circular: Renewable resources like wood or solar energy renew themselves naturally. The linear economy takes resources faster than nature can renew them.

words.meaning: A small metal pin with a spiral edge, used to hold things together.
words.circular: Fairphone holds its phones together with screws, not glue, so users can open them and replace a broken battery or camera themselves.

words.meaning: To pay to use something for a period of time without owning it.
words.circular: Leasing is part of “product-as-a-service”: you pay to use jeans or a washing machine, and the company stays responsible for repair and recycling.

words.meaning: A block of baked clay used for building walls.
words.circular: In circular construction, builders recover bricks, metal and wood from old buildings and use them again in new ones.

words.meaning: Extra; kept in case it is needed.
words.circular: Spare parts make repair possible. Under the EU Right to Repair, producers must keep spare parts available for years.

words.meaning: A thin thread of natural or artificial material (American spelling: fiber).
words.circular: Clothes made from one type of fibre are easier to recycle than blends. Washing synthetic fibres releases microplastics, so new washing machines need filters.

words.meaning: A small piece that is left over; also old metal collected for recycling.
words.circular: Food scraps can become compost or animal feed, and scrap metal can be melted down and made into new products.

words.meaning: To cut or tear something into very small pieces.
words.circular: Recycling often shreds metal or plastic into small pieces. The EU now bans companies from shredding or burning unsold clothes.

words.meaning: A person who something belongs to.
words.circular: Selling or giving a product to a new owner, for example on Vinted, keeps it in use. Renting even gives you “access over ownership”.

words.meaning: To send something through the air with your hand; “throw away” = put in the rubbish.
words.circular: The EU wants to end the “throw-away” culture. Instead of throwing things away, we can repair, share, donate or reuse them.

words.meaning: Things that are made to be sold.
words.circular: Circular goods should be durable, reusable and repairable. Destroying new, unsold goods is the worst form of the linear economy.

words.meaning: Inside, or close to the centre.
words.circular: The inner loops of the butterfly diagram – sharing, maintaining and reusing – are the best options, because they save the most energy and materials.

words.meaning: A large natural stream of water that flows to the sea.
words.circular: Textile factories can pollute rivers with dyes and chemicals, and plastic waste in rivers is carried out to the sea.

words.meaning: The liquid from fruit or vegetables.
words.circular: One orange can be used again and again: juice first, then oil from the peel, pulp for animal feed and finally compost. This is called a cascade.

words.meaning: A particular way something looks, especially in fashion.
words.circular: Fast fashion changes styles every few weeks. Slow fashion prefers timeless styles that people can wear for years.

words.meaning: A group of countries or people joined together.
words.circular: The European Union makes many circular-economy laws, such as the Right to Repair, the common charger and the ban on single-use plastics.

words.meaning: A living thing that grows in soil, like a tree or a flower.
words.circular: Plastic in the soil blocks water and plant roots and lowers harvests. Compost helps plants grow and returns nutrients to the soil.

words.meaning: A piece of clothing for a woman or girl that covers the body and legs.
words.circular: Rental services like Rent the Runway let people borrow a designer dress for a special occasion instead of buying one they wear only once.

words.meaning: To stay away from something or stop it from happening.
words.circular: Waste avoidance is the top of the waste hierarchy: the best waste is the waste that is never created.

words.meaning: A meal you eat in the middle of the day.
words.circular: School lunches can teach circular habits: right-sized portions, reusable boxes and composting leftovers for the school garden.

words.meaning: Free from dirt, marks or harmful substances.
words.circular: Recycling works best with clean, well-sorted materials. Bottles collected through a deposit system stay clean enough to become new food-grade bottles.

words.meaning: The greatest amount that is possible or allowed.
words.circular: The planetary boundaries show the ecological limits of the Earth. Six of the nine boundaries have already been crossed.

words.meaning: An area of sand or small stones next to the sea.
words.circular: Plastic bottle caps are among the top 5 items found on European beaches. That is why caps must now stay attached (tethered) to the bottle.

words.meaning: A flat piece of material that forms part of something bigger.
words.circular: Photovoltaic (solar) panels make renewable electricity. At the end of their life they need special recycling.

words.meaning: A supply of goods kept in a shop or warehouse.
words.circular: Because the EU bans destroying unsold clothes, brands have to manage their stock better and produce less.

words.meaning: The seeds of plants like wheat, rice or barley.
words.circular: Spent grain from breweries is a by-product that can become animal feed or new food instead of being thrown away.

words.meaning: Making things skilfully with your hands.
words.circular: Repair and upcycling need craft skills like sewing and fixing. The elimination of hands-on subjects at school means fewer young people learn them.

words.meaning: A fixed amount or target that must be reached.
words.circular: Recycling quotas say how much waste must be recycled. But burning plastic for energy sometimes counts towards the quota, which can be misleading.

words.meaning: Energy, especially electricity.
words.circular: A circular fashion industry should be powered by renewable energy, and food waste can be turned into biogas to power homes or vehicles.

words.meaning: A flat dish you eat food from.
words.circular: Plastic plates are banned in the EU. In France, fast-food restaurants must now serve dine-in meals on reusable plates.

words.meaning: To copy the way something looks or behaves.
words.circular: Nature has no waste – everything is used again. The biological cycle shows how a circular economy tries to mimic nature.

words.meaning: Milk and food made from milk, like cheese and yoghurt.
words.circular: Dairy by-products and other food scraps can be safely processed into animal feed instead of being wasted.

words.meaning: How fast something moves or happens.
words.circular: Fast fashion has a “need for speed”, with new collections every few weeks. Slow fashion is the antidote: fewer, better clothes worn for years.

words.meaning: A statement that something is true.
words.circular: A green claim says a product is good for the environment. If it is not true, it is greenwashing – so learn to check such claims.

words.meaning: Weighing a lot.
words.circular: Heavy metals like lead, mercury and cadmium in e-waste are toxic and must be handled safely during recycling.

words.meaning: A mixture of different things.
words.circular: Fabric blends like cotton mixed with polyester are hard to recycle. “Mono-material” clothes made of one fibre are much easier.

words.meaning: On the outside; far from the centre.
words.circular: Recycling is the outer loop of the butterfly diagram. It is better than landfill, but it destroys the product to save only the material.

words.meaning: Containing nothing.
words.circular: In a deposit return system you bring the empty bottle or can back to a reverse vending machine and get your money back.

words.meaning: Money that workers are paid for their work.
words.circular: Sustainable fashion is also about people: garment workers should get fair wages and safe working conditions.

words.meaning: A careful official check of something.
words.circular: An environmental audit checks how much waste, energy and water a company uses and where it can save resources.

words.meaning: Smoke or gas that smells strong and can be dangerous.
words.circular: Burning e-waste in the open releases toxic fumes that can travel far and harm people’s health, especially children’s.

words.meaning: Material made by weaving cotton, wool or other fibres.
words.circular: Europeans throw away about 11 kg of textiles per person every year. Old cloth can be repaired, upcycled into new items or recycled into fibres.

words.meaning: The line of bones down the middle of your back.
words.circular: The “central spine” of the butterfly diagram is the line from raw materials down to waste. The loops on both sides keep materials away from the bottom.

words.meaning: Not packed or fixed together.
words.circular: France banned plastic packaging for around 30 kinds of fruit and vegetables, so shops now sell more loose produce.

words.meaning: Work, especially hard physical work (British spelling: labour).
words.circular: Fast fashion depends on cheap labour, and child labour still exists in informal e-waste recycling. A fair circular economy protects workers.

words.meaning: The surface you walk on inside a building.
words.circular: In doughnut economics, the social floor is the minimum everyone needs (food, water, housing) and the ecological ceiling is the most the planet can take.

words.meaning: To make a hole with a machine.
words.circular: When we reuse and recycle, we do not need to mine, cut down forests or drill for new oil and gas so often.

words.meaning: Small wet cloths used for cleaning.
words.circular: Wet wipes contain plastic, so in the EU their packs must carry a warning label about the damage they do to the environment.

words.meaning: The amount of food that a farm or field produces.
words.circular: Plastic in the soil can reduce crop yields, while regenerative farming and compost keep soils healthy and productive.

words.meaning: To change something, especially to make clothes fit.
words.circular: Learning to alter and repair your own clothes helps them last longer. The most sustainable garment is the one you already own.

words.meaning: A machine for weighing things; also the size of something.
words.circular: In Finland, a bin connected to a scale shows an emoji when you throw food away – it makes food waste visible.

words.meaning: Deep holes where people dig for coal, metals or stones.
words.circular: Mining harms nature. Old smartphones are “urban mines”: some metals are more concentrated in them than in natural ores.

words.meaning: Tall plants with a wooden trunk and branches.
words.circular: Wood is renewable if forests are managed well. School projects like planting trees help biodiversity and store carbon.

words.meaning: An Italian food: flat bread with tomato, cheese and other toppings.
words.circular: The handbook explains doughnut economics with a pizza party: everyone needs at least one slice (the floor), but nobody may take ten (the ceiling).

words.meaning: Things you wear on your feet.
words.circular: The Polish company woshwosh cleans and repairs shoes and has given a second life to over 550,000 pairs.

words.meaning: Pieces that together make a machine or object.
words.circular: Modular design lets you replace only the broken part, like a phone battery or camera, instead of the whole device.

words.meaning: A very large sea animal.
words.circular: The EU common charger saves about 11,000 tonnes of e-waste a year – about the weight of 70 blue whales!

words.meaning: A small amount of food eaten between meals.
words.circular: Upcycled snacks use leftovers, such as fruit pulp from juice factories, to make new, healthy food.

words.meaning: A flat piece of material; a circuit board holds the electronic parts of a device.
words.circular: Circuit boards in phones and computers contain gold, silver, platinum and palladium, so they are valuable to recycle.

words.meaning: Substances like air that are neither solid nor liquid.
words.circular: Greenhouse gases cause climate change. About half of global emissions come from extracting and processing raw materials.

words.meaning: A thin, flat piece cut from something bigger.
words.circular: In the pizza-party example, the “floor” means everyone gets at least one slice, so nobody goes hungry.

words.meaning: Covered with dirt or marks; not clean.
words.circular: Dirty or wrongly sorted waste contaminates recycling. Bottles returned for a deposit are not mixed with dirty trash, so they recycle well.

words.meaning: Plants grown by farmers, like wheat, corn or vegetables.
words.circular: Some crops are never harvested because prices are too low or the vegetables look “ugly”. This is food loss – before the food even reaches a shop.

words.meaning: Stuck together with glue.
words.circular: Many smartphones are glued shut, so they are almost impossible to repair. Circular design uses screws instead of glue.

words.meaning: Materials like coal, oil or gas that are burned for energy.
words.circular: Plastics and synthetic fibres like polyester are made from fossil fuels, so they add to greenhouse gas emissions.

words.meaning: The food eaten at one time, like breakfast or dinner.
words.circular: Apps like Too Good To Go and food banks rescue meals that shops and restaurants would otherwise throw away.

words.meaning: Lines of rock or coral just under the surface of the sea.
words.circular: Plastic debris smothers coral reefs and mangroves and reduces the variety of life in the ocean.

words.meaning: The top layer of earth in which plants grow.
words.circular: Regenerative farming and compost rebuild soils, while plastic waste and chemicals damage them.

words.meaning: The range or area that something covers.
words.circular: “Scope 3 emissions” are all the emissions in a company’s supply chain. They are hard to measure but often the biggest part.
